title: Wet-State Evolution of Oil-Mist Coalescing Filters and Its Implications for Service-Life Evaluation
content: Oil-mist coalescing filters are commonly compared using filtration efficiency and pressure drop from short tests, although retained liquid continues to redistribute during operation. This critical review examines how liquid morphology, distribution and connectivity affect the interpretation of wet performance and service-life evidence. Imaging reveals substantial local saturation differences and extensive inter-fiber liquid structures. Within one hybrid–Janus comparison, whole-filter saturation ranged from 54.47% to 61.96%, whereas source-reported wet-to-clean pressure-drop ratios ranged from 3.32 to 22.36. These observations support considering liquid arrangement alongside bulk inventory, but do not isolate connectivity from pore geometry and wettability. Long-duration experiments also show that drainage can coexist with pressure-drop creep over 1100 h. We distinguish measured endpoints, observation durations and lifetime estimates extrapolated from short degradation records. A traceable service-life claim requires defined loading and operating conditions, concurrent resistance and outlet measurements, an explicit endpoint, and separation of measured duration from predicted life. A proposed reporting framework and a conditional pressure-scaling analysis identify the evidence needed to assess transfer from laboratory media to compressed-air cartridges.
